posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: Say I was going to build a new house. How do you think I should I design a holography lab into it? Even if money is no problem. Money is a problem but holography more important.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
I would need two rooms. One 6 feet larger than the table in both directions. So for a 4 x 10' table the room would be 10 x 16'. This room would be placed under positive pressure with HEPA filtration. It would be painted flat black or better yet Thelo Violet. There would be the sets of lighting, one bright safe light for loading film. One dim safe light aimed at the floor for walking in and out of the room and white light for setup. At one end of the room would be 1' deep shelving with glass doors from floor to ceiling to store optics.

The other room would be 8x8' and have a commercial stainless 3 basin sink from a bar. (Triple Dip is the industry name.) Next to the sink and on the adjacent wall would be kitchen counters. On the wall behind the sink would be a HEPA work station. Next to the HEPA work station would be a counter with an exhaust hood above from a commercial stove. A small electric oven built into one of the counters would be helpful as would as many cabinets as would fit.

Well, this would be a start...

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: Put the lab in an unheated sub-basement, ideally completely encased in concrete with insulated trapdoor entry and filtered air intake as recommended by Colin. Pretend its a fallout shelter Build in a geologically stable area, far from major traffic arteries. Stock up on several month's supply of canned food and lentils so you won't have to leave the lab to fight off mutant zombies until your holograms are perfected.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
LOL Bob, that's great.

Ido have to agree 100% that a basement completely below ground is the best. What I would also do is instead of pouring a concrete slab for the flour and putting the table ont that, I would put in 6 footers (concrete and block) that go down about 3 feet below the basement gound for table columns. Then pour you concrete floor around those columns with rubber separating the floor and the columns. Then any vibration dampening table set on those columns are pretty independent of vibrations from the house.

Boy Grandpa Munster had it made, didn't he?

posts.author: Kiffdino
posts.content_md:
On national geographic TV I once saw a documentary on an US ARMY nuclear bomb shelter built into some mountain.

They dug a hole into the mountain and built the bunker inside resting on gigantic springs.

So if a nuke hit it, there would be less vibration.

They could make pretty sweet holograms in there i guess.
